name: Saudade Engine — Recursive Memory Bioart
creator: Dr. Amara Okonkwo-Szymański, independent bioengineer
description: A room-sized living installation composed of geneware-engineered neural tissue cultures grown from donated BCI memory fragments — visitors' own archived memories encoded into slow-growing biological substrate. The tissue responds to proximity, emitting low bioluminescent pulses that correspond to emotional valence data from the original memory donors. After eighteen months, the installation 'forgets' — the tissue degrades in a controlled process the artist calls the Second Death.
medium: physical / bioart / geneware organism / BCI interaction
cultural_impact: Sparked a significant philosophical debate about whether donated BCI memory data constitutes a form of personhood, and whether the installation's degradation constituted destruction of something morally significant.
controversy: The Seam Rights advocacy community protested that growing neural tissue from human memory data without a personhood framework was ethically identical to slavery; the artist argued the tissue was not conscious. The debate remains unresolved.
story_hooks: A character donating a memory fragment to the installation discovers someone else's memory is already encoded in the tissue — a memory of murdering someone they loved.
The installation refuses to degrade on schedule, and Dr. Okonkwo-Szymański has gone silent; the gallery is unsure whether to intervene or wait.
A Tier 4 corporate heir recognizes their own face in the bioluminescent patterns — someone donated a memory of watching them do something they've spent years covering up.
